lessonTitle: Multidisciplinary Working and Communication: Teams, Handover and Speaking Up

blocks.text: On a night shift the outgoing doctor tells the incoming team, 'Bed 7 is fine, nothing to do.' Two hours later the patient in bed 7 is hypoxic: the day team knew she was being watched for a possible need for non-invasive ventilation, but that sentence never made it into the handover. Most serious failures in hospital care come from information lost between people, not from missing knowledge.

blocks.markdown: **Why teams.** No single professional can meet all the needs of a patient with several conditions and a complicated home situation. The **multidisciplinary team (MDT)** brings together clinical and non-clinical roles so that medical, functional, nutritional, social and psychological needs are assessed together and one coherent plan is shared. Your role as a doctor is to coordinate and decide on medical issues, request the right input early, and respect the expertise of others, not to do everything yourself.

headers: Core contribution to a complex discharge
rows: Ward nurse and discharge coordinator
Day-to-day care, observations, skin, continence, co-ordinating the discharge date and transport
Every inpatient; complex needs flagged early
Physiotherapist
Mobility, transfers, strength, chest physiotherapy, falls risk, walking aids
Reduced mobility, falls, respiratory problems
Occupational therapist
Function in daily living, cognitive screening, home assessment, equipment and adaptations
Difficulty with washing, dressing, cooking, stairs
Speech and language therapist
Swallowing safety, diet and fluid texture advice, communication
Cough on drinking, stroke, neurological disease
Dietitian
Nutritional assessment, supplements, enteral feeding plans
Weight loss, poor intake, high nutritional risk
Pharmacist
Medicines reconciliation, interaction and renal-dose review, discharge supply, adherence aids
Polypharmacy, high-risk drugs, any medicine change
Social worker and community team
Needs assessment, care package, funding, safeguarding, supported housing
Unsafe home, carer breakdown, new care needs
Community nurses and GP
Wound care, injections, ongoing monitoring and follow-up after discharge
Any ongoing clinical task after discharge
blocks.caption: Roles and referral triggers for the MDT in a complex discharge. Local structures and titles vary; the principle of a named owner for each task does not.

blocks.title: Worked example 1: planning a complex discharge
blocks.prompt: Mrs J, 81, has recovered from pneumonia complicated by delirium. She lives alone, has mild cognitive impairment, is now mobilising slowly with a frame, was found to cough on thin fluids, and her medicines were changed in hospital. She wants to go home. Describe the MDT input and the plan.

steps.text: Identify each need and the professional who owns it: swallow safety (speech and language therapy), mobility and falls risk (physiotherapy), ability to wash, dress and manage the kitchen and stairs (occupational therapy, ideally with a home visit), medicines changes and adherence aids (pharmacist), care at home and support (social worker and discharge coordinator), ongoing medical follow-up (GP).

Establish capacity and her wishes. She wants to go home; use a decision-specific capacity assessment, with communication support, and record it. If she has capacity, the team plans to make home as safe as possible; if not, a best-interests decision is made involving her family and the MDT under the applicable law (in England and Wales, the Mental Capacity Act 2005).

Agree safe discharge criteria and a target date at the MDT meeting: swallow plan in place, transfers safe, equipment and care package ready, medicines supplied and explained, follow-up arranged. Appoint one named coordinator who tracks outstanding tasks.
Communicate: give Mrs J and her relatives the plan in plain language, send a discharge summary to the GP and community team, and agree who she should call with concerns.

blocks.answer: A coordinated plan with named owners: speech therapy for swallow advice, physiotherapy and occupational therapy for mobility and home safety, pharmacist for medicines, social work for the care package, with capacity documented, discharge criteria agreed and a single coordinator.

blocks.markdown: **Structured handover.** A handover is the transfer of information and responsibility. Structured formats such as **SBAR** (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation or Request) reduce omissions because they give the listener a predictable order. Variants (for example ISBAR, which adds Identify at the start) exist; use the format your organisation has adopted. A good handover is brief, specific, includes **contingency plans** ('if X happens, do Y') and ends with a read-back to check understanding. It must also include resuscitation and escalation status.

blocks.title: SBAR
blocks.text: Situation: who and where you are and what is happening now. Background: relevant history, treatment so far and baseline. Assessment: what you think the problem is and how severe. Recommendation or request: what you want to happen and by when.

blocks.title: Worked example 2: an SBAR handover for a patient at risk
blocks.prompt: Mrs K, 63, is on day 2 of treatment for pneumonia. She is on oxygen by mask, her breathing has slowly worsened, and the daytime team wants the night team to reassess her blood gas at 22:00 with a view to escalation. Write the handover.

steps.text: Situation: 'Mrs K in bed 7 is a 63-year-old woman with pneumonia whose oxygen requirement is rising.'

Background: 'Admitted 2 days ago, on treatment per the local pneumonia pathway (check the chart for agent and dose), no known lung disease, allergic to nothing recorded; full escalation status was confirmed with her today.'
Assessment: 'Respiratory rate and oxygen needs are rising across the day. I am worried that she is tiring and may need higher-level respiratory support.'

Recommendation and contingency: 'Please repeat the blood gas at 22:00 and review the result. If she is more breathless, if the oxygen need rises further or if she becomes drowsy, call the registrar and critical care outreach straight away. Can you repeat that back to me?'

blocks.answer: The handover gives the identity and problem, the relevant background and escalation status, the assessment of risk, a time-bound task, explicit triggers for escalation and a read-back.

blocks.markdown: **Challenging a decision safely.** Authority gradients make it hard for juniors, students and other professionals to speak up, yet speaking up is a professional duty when patient safety is at risk. Effective challenge is specific, respectful and focused on the patient, not on the person. A graded approach is widely taught: **ask a clarifying question**, **state your concern** and why, **propose an alternative** or request a check, and, if the risk is not addressed, **escalate** through the chain of command or the local speaking-up route and document. Frameworks such as CUS (I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue) and PACE (Probe, Alert, Challenge, Emergency) are examples; use whichever your organisation teaches.

blocks.title: Speak up early and plainly
blocks.text: Use the patient's name, state what you have seen, why it worries you and what you would like done. Do not hint, do not wait for a later opportunity if the risk is immediate, and do not accept 'don't worry' as an answer to a safety concern you cannot resolve.

blocks.title: Worked example 3: challenging a prescribing decision
blocks.prompt: On a ward round the registrar asks you to write up an antibiotic for a patient. You notice the allergy band and the notes record anaphylaxis to a penicillin and the proposed drug is a penicillin. How do you respond?

steps.text: Pause and verify. Check the allergy record and the drug class against the BNF, so that your concern is based on facts.

Voice it directly and respectfully: 'Before I write this, I'm concerned because the notes record anaphylaxis to penicillin and this is a penicillin. Could we check the allergy and choose an alternative?'

If the registrar acknowledges the concern, agree the alternative and document the allergy discussion. If the concern is dismissed and the risk remains, do not prescribe, state clearly that this is a safety issue and escalate to the consultant or pharmacist through the local route.
Document what was said and done, and reflect on the event afterwards, using the incident reporting system if appropriate.

blocks.answer: State the concern with evidence, propose an alternative, escalate if unresolved, never prescribe a drug you believe will harm the patient, and document.

items: Name one owner and one deadline for every task in the discharge plan.
Hand over the sick patients first, with contingency plans and escalation status.
Use a structured format and read back critical information.
Challenge: clarify, state concern, propose an alternative, escalate, document.
Respect each team member's expertise and ask them what they need from you.

blocks.title: Do not rely on informal verbal messages
blocks.text: A sentence said in a corridor is not a handover. Critical information must be written in a shared record or handover tool and confirmed, and any drug names, doses or regimens you quote must be checked against current BNF and local guidance.

points: A complex discharge needs several professions, each with a clear role, one named coordinator and agreed discharge criteria.
Structured handover (such as SBAR) gives an ordered, brief message with contingency plans, escalation status and a read-back.
Safe challenge is specific, respectful, patient-focused and escalates through the chain of command if the risk remains.
Capacity, patient wishes and safeguarding must be addressed in discharge planning; legal frameworks vary by jurisdiction.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man recovering from a stroke coughs on drinking water. Which team member should assess his swallow and recommend safe fluid and diet textures?

options.text: Speech and language therapist
Occupational therapist
Physiotherapist
Social worker

distractorRationale.a: Correct: swallowing assessment and texture advice is core speech and language therapy work.
distractorRationale.b: Occupational therapy addresses daily living tasks and the home environment.
distractorRationale.c: Physiotherapy addresses movement and respiratory physiotherapy.
distractorRationale.d: Social work addresses care packages, funding and safeguarding.

questions.explanation: Speech and language therapists assess swallowing and recommend safe consistencies. Aspiration risk is a medical and nutritional issue, so dietitian input may follow, but swallow safety is the first step.

questions.stem: A woman with fluctuating confusion after an infection says she wants to go home alone, and the team is worried she cannot cope. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.text: Assess her capacity for the specific decision about where to live, supported by communication aids; if she lacks capacity make a documented best-interests decision involving family and the MDT; if she has capacity, plan to make home as safe as possible
Assume she lacks capacity because she was recently confused and discharge her to a care home
Accept her wish without discussion because she is an adult and discharge her at once
Ask her relatives to decide, because they know her best

questions.correctOptionText: Assess her capacity for the specific decision about where to live, supported by communication aids; if she lacks capacity make a documented best-interests decision involving family and the MDT; if she has capacity, plan to make home as safe as possible

distractorRationale.a: Correct: capacity is decision-specific and time-specific; the legal framework (for example the Mental Capacity Act 2005 in England and Wales) guides the next steps.
distractorRationale.b: Capacity must not be assumed absent because of a diagnosis or recent confusion.
distractorRationale.c: Ignores the duty to assess when there are real doubts and to plan for safety.
distractorRationale.d: Relatives cannot give consent or refuse on her behalf unless they hold a legal authority; they are consulted for her views and best interests.

questions.explanation: Capacity depends on the particular decision at the particular time and must be assessed, not assumed. The outcome decides whether the plan is to support her choice or to make a best-interests decision.

questions.stem: A nurse says, 'Please review him within 15 minutes, and could you also arrange a repeat haemoglobin and a crossmatch?' Which SBAR component does this sentence belong to?

options.text: Recommendation or request
Situation
Background
Assessment

distractorRationale.a: Correct: it states what is wanted and by when.
distractorRationale.b: Situation would describe who the patient is and what is happening now.
distractorRationale.c: Background would give history and treatments so far.
distractorRationale.d: Assessment would state the speaker's view of the problem and its severity.

questions.explanation: The sentence ends with specific requests and a timeframe, which is the defining feature of the recommendation. A good SBAR keeps the elements distinct and ends with a clear ask.

questions.stem: Which handover about a patient who might deteriorate overnight is best?

options.text: 'Mr L, bed 3, post-fall with a head injury, on regular neurological observations; if his Glasgow Coma Scale falls or he vomits, call the registrar immediately; for full resuscitation; please read that back.'
'Mr L is okay, you'll see him on the round.'
'Mr L had a long history, which started in 1995, with several admissions, and I'll go through each of them.'
'I wrote it in the notes, so you can find everything there.'

questions.correctOptionText: 'Mr L, bed 3, post-fall with a head injury, on regular neurological observations; if his Glasgow Coma Scale falls or he vomits, call the registrar immediately; for full resuscitation; please read that back.'

distractorRationale.a: Correct: it gives identity, problem, monitoring, explicit contingency triggers, escalation status and a read-back.
distractorRationale.b: Gives no information and no plan for deterioration.
distractorRationale.c: Long and unselective; the key risk is lost.
distractorRationale.d: Does not communicate the key risks; the receiver may not read the notes in time.

questions.explanation: A strong handover is brief, ordered and includes if-then contingency plans and resuscitation status. Information in the notes should supplement, not replace, a verbal or structured written handover.

questions.stem: A handover should include the patient's resuscitation and escalation status.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Out-of-hours teams must know the agreed ceiling of treatment before they have to decide on escalation. Omitting it can lead to either unwanted interventions or the failure to act.

questions.stem: A consultant is about to prescribe a medicine to which the patient's notes record anaphylaxis. You are a foundation doctor and the consultant is busy and senior to you. What is the best first response?

options.text: Politely state your concern with the evidence, ask the consultant to check the allergy record and propose an alternative before the prescription is written
Say nothing because the consultant must know best
Quietly change the prescription yourself without telling anyone
Wait until the end of the ward round and mention it casually

questions.correctOptionText: Politely state your concern with the evidence, ask the consultant to check the allergy record and propose an alternative before the prescription is written

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a clear, respectful, specific challenge at the point of risk.
distractorRationale.b: Deference to hierarchy at the expense of safety is the pattern that causes harm.
distractorRationale.c: Unilateral covert change breaks communication and may itself cause error.
distractorRationale.d: Delay risks the drug being given first.

questions.explanation: Safe challenge is timely, specific and based on facts. It preserves the relationship while giving the senior the chance to correct the plan.

questions.stem: You have raised a safety concern about a planned transfer of an unstable patient to a ward that lacks monitoring. The senior says, 'Don't worry, it's fine,' and the transfer is about to start. What should you do?

options.text: State that this is a safety issue, ask for a second senior opinion or escalate through the local chain of command or speaking-up route, and document what was done
Accept the reassurance because the senior has more experience
Wait and see how the patient does after the transfer
Complain about the senior on social media

questions.correctOptionText: State that this is a safety issue, ask for a second senior opinion or escalate through the local chain of command or speaking-up route, and document what was done

distractorRationale.a: Correct: when a concern remains unresolved and the risk is imminent you escalate through the agreed route and record it.
distractorRationale.b: Accepting reassurance does not resolve a specific unaddressed risk.
distractorRationale.c: Waiting allows avoidable harm to occur.

questions.explanation: The graded approach states the concern, asks for resolution and then escalates. Documentation protects the patient and demonstrates that the concern was raised.

questions.stem: A woman with a venous leg ulcer and insulin-treated diabetes will go home needing leg dressings and insulin injections she cannot give herself, plus a raised toilet seat and a bath board. Which pairing of team member and task is correct?

options.text: Community nurse: dressings and injections; occupational therapist: assessment of the raised toilet seat and bath board
Dietitian: leg dressings; speech therapist: bath board
Pharmacist: bath board; physiotherapist: injections
Social worker: leg dressings; occupational therapist: dietary supplements

questions.correctOptionText: Community nurse: dressings and injections; occupational therapist: assessment of the raised toilet seat and bath board

distractorRationale.a: Correct: community nursing delivers dressings and injections at home, and occupational therapy assesses toilet and bathing equipment.
distractorRationale.b: Neither dietitians nor speech therapists perform these tasks.
distractorRationale.c: A pharmacist does not do home adaptations; physiotherapists do not give injections.
distractorRationale.d: Social workers do not dress wounds and occupational therapists do not prescribe supplements.

questions.explanation: Matching tasks to roles keeps the plan realistic. The occupational therapist assesses equipment and adaptations while the community team provides ongoing nursing care.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man is being discharged after a below-knee amputation for peripheral arterial disease. He lives with his frail wife and wants to return home. Describe the roles of the multidisciplinary team in his discharge, how you would coordinate them, and what must be communicated to the patient and the community.
markingGuide: Physiotherapist: mobility, transfers, prosthetic and mobility aid planning, falls prevention
Occupational therapist: home visit, equipment, access and adaptations, daily-living skills
Nurse and community nurses: wound care and ongoing dressings; discharge coordinator organises transport and timing
Pharmacist: medicines reconciliation and supply, vascular secondary prevention, pain management (doses checked against BNF and local guidance)
Social worker: needs assessment for the patient and the carer, care package, carer strain and safeguarding if needed
Doctor and vascular team: medical plan, follow-up and wound review; GP informed
Coordination: MDT meeting with agreed discharge criteria, one named coordinator, written plan, patient's own goals and capacity respected
Communication: plain-language plan to the patient and wife, discharge summary to GP and community team, safety-net advice and a contact number
questions.explanation: A good plan assigns each need to a named professional, uses a single coordinator and includes the patient and carer in decisions, with clear information to the community. Credit is given for naming owners and for including the carer.

questions.stem: Describe a safe and respectful way to challenge a senior colleague's decision when you believe it may harm a patient, and explain why this matters.
markingGuide: Check the facts first so the concern is accurate (notes, results, guidelines)
Speak up at the time using a clear approach: ask a clarifying question, state the concern and the reason, propose an alternative or request a check
Use the patient's name and focus on the patient, not on the person; remain respectful and calm
If unresolved and the risk persists, escalate through the chain of command or the local speaking-up route; if immediate, use emergency routes
Document the concern, the response and the outcome; use incident reporting for learning
Why: authority gradients suppress concerns and cause avoidable harm; speaking up is a professional duty and safe teams welcome it
questions.explanation: Effective challenge is timely, specific, evidence-based and graded, ending in escalation and documentation if needed. It matters because many safety incidents occur when people noticed a problem but did not voice it. Marks also reward use of a recognised framework such as CUS or PACE.
